legend: Ridham's birthday is coming up and he really loves primes and permutations. Knowing this Aastik decided to gift Ridham a permutation a$$$a$$$ of length n$$$n$$$ such that ai+an−i+1$$$a_i + a_{n-i+1}$$$ is prime for all i$$$i$$$ such that 1≤i≤n$$$1 \le i \le n$$$, but just when Aastik sat down to generate this permutation he realised that he did not know how to make such a permutation. Help Aastik to prepare the gift for Ridham.

A permutation of length n$$$n$$$ is an array consisting of n$$$n$$$ distinct integers from 1$$$1$$$ to n$$$n$$$ in arbitrary order. For example, [2,3,1,5,4]$$$[2,3,1,5,4]$$$ is a permutation, but [1,2,2]$$$[1,2,2]$$$ is not a permutation (2$$$2$$$ appears twice in the array), and [1,3,4]$$$[1,3,4]$$$ is also not a permutation (n=3$$$n = 3$$$ but there is 4$$$4$$$ in the array).
input: The first line contains a single integer t$$$t$$$ (1≤t≤104$$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$). The description of the test cases follows.
The first line and only line of each test case contains an integer n$$$n$$$ (1≤n≤106$$$1 \le n \le 10^6$$$) — the size of the permutation a$$$a$$$.
The sum of n$$$n$$$ over all testcases does not exceed 3⋅106$$$3 \cdot 10^6$$$.
output: For each testcase, output n$$$n$$$ integers — the elements of the required permutation. If it's not possible, output −1$$$-1$$$.
